title: Marker-Assisted Selection, Genomic Selection and Prediction Limits

content.overview: Modern breeding can use markers linked to major loci or genome-wide marker data to predict breeding value, but prediction accuracy comes from well-designed training populations and phenotypes. Genomics does not eliminate the need to measure plants.

vocabulary.definition: Selection using markers associated with specific genes or genomic regions linked to target traits.
Prediction of breeding value using many markers distributed across the genome, usually through a trained statistical model.
A population with both genotype and phenotype data used to estimate or train a genomic prediction model.

sections.title: Marker-assisted selection works best when associations are robust
sections.body: Markers linked to well-characterized loci can support early selection, but linkage, population structure and genetic background can affect whether an association transfers to new germplasm.

sections.title: Genomic selection depends on phenotype quality
sections.body: Genome-wide prediction requires sufficiently large, representative training populations with reliable trait data. Poor phenotype records produce weak prediction regardless of sequencing depth.

sections.title: Validation must match the target population and environment
sections.body: Complex cannabis traits often show polygenic architecture and G×E. Models and marker associations should be validated in the germplasm and environments where selections will be used.

workedExamples: A marker discovered in fiber hemp should not automatically be assumed predictive in unrelated high-cannabinoid germplasm.
A genomic model trained in one narrow population may lose accuracy when applied to genetically distant lines or different environments.
commonMistakes: Treating marker association as causal proof.
Building prediction models from inconsistent phenotype records.
Assuming genomic selection removes the need for field or controlled-environment validation.
content.practicalApplication: Before using a marker or prediction model, document discovery population, trait definition, marker coverage, training size, phenotype quality, validation population and expected decision error.
content.summary: Genomics can accelerate breeding, but it amplifies the quality of the underlying data. Strong phenotyping, representative populations and independent validation remain essential.
